clinicalPearls: Asbestosis is a diffuse interstitial fibrosis of the lung caused by inhaled asbestos fibres, and typically requires substantial cumulative exposure with a long latency of many years
Progressive exertional breathlessness with a dry cough, fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles and sometimes finger clubbing are characteristic findings
It must be distinguished from pleural plaques and benign pleural disease, which indicate exposure but are not the fibrosing lung disease itself
Asbestos exposure markedly increases the risk of both bronchial carcinoma and malignant pleural mesothelioma, and this risk is central to counselling and follow-up
Smoking multiplies the lung cancer risk in asbestos-exposed workers, so cessation advice is a key intervention
High-resolution CT is more sensitive than plain radiography for detecting early fibrosis and coexisting pleural changes
There is no treatment that reverses the fibrosis, so care is supportive and centred on preventing further exposure and managing complications
A careful occupational history covering construction, shipbuilding, insulation and demolition work is essential, and cases usually have medicolegal and compensation implications
reference.pathophysiology: Inhaled asbestos fibres that reach the distal airways and alveoli are incompletely cleared and provoke chronic macrophage-driven inflammation with release of reactive oxygen species and fibrogenic mediators. This leads to progressive deposition of collagen and diffuse interstitial fibrosis, initially in the lower zones, impairing gas exchange and lung compliance. The same persistent fibre burden and cellular injury underlie the associated malignant risks of mesothelioma and lung cancer.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest to characterise fibrosis and pleural disease
Chest radiography using standardised pneumoconiosis reading
Pulmonary function tests showing a restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer
Detailed lifetime occupational and exposure history
Investigation of any new or worsening symptoms for malignancy, including mesothelioma
redFlags: New or worsening breathlessness, chest pain or pleural effusion raising concern for mesothelioma
Haemoptysis or a new lung mass suggesting bronchial carcinoma
Unexplained weight loss in an asbestos-exposed worker
reference.prognosis: Asbestosis tends to progress slowly and is irreversible; the overall outlook is dominated by the substantially raised lifetime risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma, which are the leading causes of death in exposed individuals.
pitfalls: Confusing pleural plaques with asbestosis and mislabelling exposure markers as the fibrosing disease
Failing to emphasise smoking cessation given the multiplicative lung cancer risk
Missing an evolving malignancy by attributing new symptoms to known fibrosis
Overlooking the need for a documented occupational history for compensation
Assuming a short exposure excludes disease when latency is prolonged
management: Complete cessation of asbestos exposure and full smoking cessation to reduce the multiplicative lung-cancer risk, as no drug reverses the established fibrosis
Supportive respiratory care with pulmonary rehabilitation, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, and long-term oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia
Prompt treatment of intercurrent respiratory infections and management of any secondary pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale
Structured surveillance for malignancy, with a low threshold to investigate new breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss or a pleural effusion for bronchial carcinoma and mesothelioma
Referral to occupational medicine for exposure documentation, medico-legal assessment and eligibility for industrial-injury compensation
Multidisciplinary respiratory follow-up using serial lung function and high-resolution CT to track progression
